tier_reason: The opening post of sequoia-pgp/sequoia issue #771 shows exactly the four quoted runs (sq 51.4 and 128.0 MB/s, gpg 138.7 and 170.7 MB/s) as one-shot terminal output with no versions, CPU or repetitions; a later comment adds an independent run with versions and CPU, but the numbers are from 2021, the baseline was sped up days later, and there is no benchmark code or build flags, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Binary output: gpg 170.7 MB/s (6 s) vs sq 128.0 MB/s (8 s), 1.33x (derived from page data). ASCII-armored output: gpg 138.7 MB/s (10 s) vs sq 51.4 MB/s (27 s), 2.70x (derived from page data). A third-party comment in the same issue (jgoerzen, 2021-11-01) timed binary encryption of a 3.3 GB file with AES256 forced on both tools: gpg 2.2.27 (Debian bullseye) 16.97 s vs sq 0.25.0 (sequoia-openpgp 1.5.0) 36.60 s on an Intel Core i5-5200U, 2.16x (derived from page data). All figures are from November 2021.
corrections.caveats: The issue (gitlab.com sequoia-pgp/sequoia #771, opened 2021-11-01, still open, no labels) was filed by Sequoia developer Justus Winter (teythoon) against his own project, so the comparison comes from the baseline's maintainers, not from GnuPG; the opening post gives no gpg or sq version, key type, cipher or CPU and is a single run per configuration. The numbers are stale: the armored gap was traced to Sequoia's slow CRC24 in the armor encoder (issue #772, closed by commit aeacd64d on 2021-11-05), and a maintainer called binary encryption 'a bit slower, but in the same order of magnitude'. The same thread shows the decryption ranking reversed after Sequoia's buffer fixes and XXH3 body hashing (2021-11-04: gpg 10.944 s vs sq 9.264 s decrypting a 3 GB binary message), so GnuPG is not faster on decryption. No newer gpg-versus-sq throughput comparison was found (one WebSearch); whether current sq still trails gpg on encryption is unknown. The dd from /dev/urandom pipeline can itself cap throughput near the quoted figures, and the armored gap measures the armor encoder rather than the cipher. GnuPG's own NEWS lists only self-versus-earlier-release speedups (signature verification more than four times faster, detached signing doubled, threefold decryption speedup for large files, AES256.OCB encryption nearly doubled) with no external baseline. The GitHub repo is a mirror the maintainers do not track (canonical git.gnupg.org). Category aead-and-ciphers fits bulk public-key encryption throughput better than the suggested signatures-kem.

notes: Numbers verified verbatim in the GitLab issue (opened via the GitLab API and discussions JSON). Shortcomings: comparison filed by the baseline's own developer, single unversioned runs, November 2021 numbers on sq 0.25 that Sequoia fixed days later (armor CRC24 fix #772; decryption now faster than gpg in the same thread), no benchmark code or flags, and Sequoia is a challenger rather than an incumbent baseline. GitHub mirror metadata checked: 991 stars, GPL-3.0 plus other licence files, last commit 2026-10-09, not archived.

tier_reason: result.json in scc-tw/cryptobench-cpp contains the BM_MbedTLS_* and BM_OpenSSL_* rows with the quoted 64-byte means (211.66 vs 163.95, 197.00 vs 160.93, 168.53 vs 135.30 MB/s) and the reversal from 256 B up; benchmark code and README flags are public, but no compiler name or version and no CPU model are recorded, and the 0-star suite is not a well-known independent shootout, so C.

corrections.caveats: Harvested shootout row, not a claim Mbed TLS makes: the README and ChangeLog contain no comparison with OpenSSL, and Mbed TLS is the slower library for every hash, HMAC and CBC row and for AEAD at 256 B and above (OpenSSL 1.05x faster for AES-128-GCM at 256 B, 4.66x at 16384 B, 7840.4 vs 1683.0 MB/s; ChaCha20-Poly1305 3.79x at 16384 B, derived from page data). The benchmark owner's repo (scc-tw/cryptobench-cpp, MIT) has 0 stars and 39 commits and one local laptop run (2025-11-05) with no CPU model or compiler version; the context block shows a load average of 3.6 to 4.3 on the 8-CPU host during the run, so the machine was not idle. The 64-byte advantage reflects per-call overhead rather than cipher speed: src/adapters/openssl_adapter.cpp calls EVP_CIPHER_CTX_new, two EVP_EncryptInit_ex calls with an implicit EVP_aes_128_gcm() fetch, and EVP_CIPHER_CTX_free on every message, while src/adapters/mbedtls_adapter.cpp runs psa_import_key, allocates a std::vector, copies the output with two memcpy calls and destroys the key per message. In the same file every OpenSSL public-key row and Botan's AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-256-CBC rows are error rows ('Key generation failed', 'Encryption failed' and similar), so OpenSSL is the only peer for this comparison. A wolfSSL vendor benchmark (WebSearch snippet only, page not opened) reports wolfCrypt well ahead of Mbed TLS 3.6.6; no source reached shows Mbed TLS ahead of OpenSSL on bulk throughput.

notes: All quoted numbers and the flip at 256 B confirmed in result.json; adapter code confirms the per-call EVP context setup that explains OpenSSL's 64-byte loss. Shortcomings: win only at 64-byte messages in a per-call setup-dominated harness, OpenSSL faster at every larger size and for every hash, HMAC and CBC row, single noisy laptop run with no CPU model or compiler version, 0-star benchmark repo. Mbed TLS metadata checked: 7.0k stars, Apache-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-or-later, last commit 2026-10-07 on development, not archived.
